name: Question 11
problem:
Which of the following functions are piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1]?$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}2x-\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}, & x<0 \\ x+\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}}, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}\,,\,g(x)=4x-\sqrt[7]{{x}^{3}},\,h(x)=3{x}^{2}+\sqrt[5]{{x}^{3}}
$$
worked_solution:
A function $f(x)$ is **piecewise smooth** on $x\in [a,b]$ if

- $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous on $[a,b],$ and

- ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists and is continuous except possibly at finitely many points, where its one-sided limits exist and are finite.

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $f(x)$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ We split the interval at $x=0.$ On the open intervals $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ we have

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}2x-{x}^{2/3}, & x<0 \\ x+{x}^{2/5}, & x>0\end{aligned}\,,
$$

so

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\begin{aligned}2-\frac{2}{3{x}^{1/3}}, & x<0 \\ 1+\frac{2}{5{x}^{3/5}}, & x>0\end{aligned}
$$

While this derivative is continuous on the open pieces $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ the limits of the derivative as $x\to 0$ are not finite. In fact, the derivative becomes unbounded near $x=0.$ Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

- The function $g(x)=4x-\sqrt[7]{{x}^{3}}$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ We split the interval at $x=0$ into the two open intervals $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1).$ For $x\ne 0,$

$$
g(x)=4x-{x}^{3/7},
$$

so

$$
{g}^{′}(x)=4-\frac{3}{7{x}^{4/7}}.
$$

While this derivative is continuous on the open pieces $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ the limits of the derivative as $x\to 0$ are not finite. In fact, the derivative becomes unbounded near $x=0.$ Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

- The function $h(x)=3{x}^{2}+\sqrt[5]{{x}^{3}}$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ We split the interval at $x=0$ into the two open intervals $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1).$ For $x\ne 0,$

$$
h(x)=3{x}^{2}+{x}^{3/5},
$$

so

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=6x+\frac{3}{5{x}^{2/5}}.
$$

While this derivative is continuous on the open pieces $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ the limits of the derivative as $x\to 0$ are not finite. In fact, the derivative becomes unbounded near $x=0.$ Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the functions."
